Society during China’s Golden Age

600–1300 | Who Shared in the Prosperity?

8
BIG QUESTION

Golden age China grew rich from trade, cities, and farming. But who actually shared in that prosperity? To what extent did people at every level of society benefit?

Part 1 of 5

How to Read a Source

Step 1Who, Purpose, Audience, Point of View

Historians never take a source at face value. Before you read, ask who made it, why, and for whom. This assignment has two kinds of sources: primary sources made during the golden age itself (paintings and poems) and Historian’s Voices, excerpts from modern historians who study that time.

WHO · Who created this source? What was their job or social class? Position shapes what a person sees and what they leave out.

PURPOSE · Why was it made? To record, praise, persuade, or complain? Purpose affects what is included or exaggerated.

AUDIENCE · Who was it made for? Creators adjust their message to the people they expect to see or read it.

POINT OF VIEW · Whose experience is shown? Whose is missing? Few farmers or women wrote their own accounts, so we must read carefully.

As you read: look for details that show wealth, comfort, or opportunity, and details that show hardship or limits on people’s lives.

Word help: primary source = made by someone alive at the time · Historian’s Voice = a modern historian’s analysis · point of view = the position someone sees from

Work on your own. Everything you need is in this reading.

Station A: Cities and Merchants

BackgroundCities and Merchants

During the Tang and Song dynasties, China’s cities and trade grew enormously, and a few cities held a million people. Confucian officials, however, distrusted merchants as people who made nothing yet grew rich. Source A shows one crossroads in a Song-era city. Voice A explains how the place of merchants was changing.

Source AAlong the River during the Qingming Festival (detail)

Zhang Zeduan, 12th century. One section of a much larger handscroll showing a busy crossroads in an unidentified city.

What to look for: Look at shops and signs, people carrying loads, animals and carts, and the different kinds of people in the street.

Zhang Zeduan, Along the River during the Qingming Festival, 12th century. Primary source.

Historian’s Voice AMorris Rossabi on the Place of Merchants in Chinese Society

Morris Rossabi writes about the Southern Song period, 1127–1279.

Merchants were no longer limited to the capitals of specific counties and thus traded in small towns and villages as well. Although government officials continued to supervise markets, merchants faced fewer restrictions in trade. Enclosed markets became rarer, allowing merchants to trade in neighborhoods that had earlier had restricted commercial areas. . . .
Commercialization created a prosperous merchant class but . . . despite their wealth, merchants did not have commensurate political power. A strong state that valued agriculture above all other economic pursuits did not permit much leverage to merchants and suppressed any assertions of merchant independence. . . . In addition, wealthy merchants would, on occasion, buy land as a possible first step toward their families’ eventual acceptance as part of the gentry. They also would aspire to have sons who passed the civil-service examinations.

Excerpted from Morris Rossabi, A History of China (Oxford: Wiley Blackwell, 2014), 202–3.

Station B: Life in the Countryside

BackgroundLife in the Countryside

Most Chinese people were farmers. Confucian thinkers praised them as the source of society’s wealth, yet they paid taxes and rents, owed labor, and could be drafted into armies. We have almost no writing by farmers, so historians often turn to poems by officials. Source B has two Tang-era poems. Voice B describes a very different rural world in Song-era Fujian, a coastal province.

Source B1Po Chu-i, “Watching the Reapers”

Po Chu-i was a Tang dynasty government official and poet. He wrote this poem in 806.

Tillers of the soil have few idle months;
In the fifth month their toil is double-fold.
A south-wind visits the fields at night:
Suddenly the hill is covered with yellow corn.
Wives and daughters shoulder baskets of rice;
Youths and boys carry the flasks of wine.
Following after they bring a wage of meat,
To the strong reapers toiling on the southern hill,
Whose feet are burned by the hot earth they tread,
Whose backs are scorched by flames of the shining sky.
Tired they toil, caring nothing for the heat,
Grudging the shortness of the long summer day.
A poor woman follows at the reapers’ side
With an infant child carried close at her breast.
With her right hand she gleans the fallen grain;*
In her left arm a broken basket hangs.
And I to-day . . . by virtue of what right
Have I never once tended field or tree?
My government-pay is three hundred tons;
At the year’s end I have still grain in hand.
Thinking of this, secretly I grew ashamed;
And all day the thought lingered in my head.

Arthur Waley, trans., More Translations from the Chinese (New York: Knopf, 1919), 41. *The poor were traditionally allowed to glean, that is, to gather any grain left behind in the fields after the harvest.

Source B2Du Fu, “A Song of War Chariots”

Du Fu was a Tang dynasty poet who lived in a period of frequent wars and disorder. This poem is excerpted.

The war-chariots rattle,
The war-horses whinny;
Each man of you has a bow and a quiver at his belt . . .
Father, mother, son, wife, stare at you going,
Till dust shall have buried the bridge beyond Haienyang.
We trot with them and cry and catch at their long sleeves,
But the sound of our crying goes up to the clouds;
For every time a bystander asks the men a question,
The men can only answer us that they have to go. . . .
Some of them, at fifteen sent north to guard the river,
At forty were sent west to cultivate the border.
The mayor wound their turbans for them when they started out.
And they’re at the front though their turbaned hair is white,
At the front where the blood of men spills like the sea—
And still the heart of Emperor Wu is lifted up for war.
Do you know that, east of the mountain, in two hundred districts
And in thousands of villages, only weeds grow
And though strong women plough, the rows are all broken? . . .
We have learned now that to have a boy is bad luck—
And having a girl is very much better,
Who marries and lives in the house of a neighbor,
While under the sod we bury our boys . . .

Excerpted from Du Fu, “A Song of War Chariots,” in The Bookman (New York: George H. Doran, 1921), 568.

Historian’s Voice BValerie Hansen on the Social Implications of the Commercializing Economy

Valerie Hansen writes about Fujian province in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

China’s international contacts were so extensive that they affected people at all social levels—not just the residents of Chinese port cities but also those living deep in the hinterland. . . .
The prosperity of Quanzhou and other nearby ports spilled over to the entire province of Fujian, enabling the province’s residents to shift away from subsistence farming so that they could produce goods for commercial markets. . . . They stopped growing their own food. They discovered that they could make more money if they cultivated cash crops . . . or if they grew local textile fibers. . . . They came to purchase food for their families at local markets. . . . Many gave up agriculture altogether. . . .
The ceramics industry absorbed the largest share of the labor force. Entrepreneurs built dragon kilns. . . . [S]uch kilns employed hundreds, if not thousands, of laborers. . . . [S]ome 375,000 people were involved in making export ceramics in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

Excerpted from Valerie Hansen, The Year 1000: When Explorers Connected the World—and Globalization Began (New York: Scribner, 2020), 199, 216.

Question 5 · Point of View. (2 pts) Po Chu-i and Du Fu were government officials, not farmers. How might that shape what they notice and how they describe farm families? Why can their poems still be useful to a historian?

Station C: The Scholar Elite

BackgroundThe Scholar Elite

At the top of society stood scholar-officials, men who passed the civil service exams and ran the government. Source C shows scholar-officials drinking tea and wine with the emperor. It is usually attributed to Emperor Huizong, a skilled painter and poet who was criticized for paying more attention to art than to ruling. In 1127 he was captured by the Jin, a nomadic people from the north.

Source CScholars Gathering in a Bamboo Garden

12th century. Painting usually attributed to Emperor Huizong.

What to look for: Look at the setting, the table, the clothing, and the people who are serving.

Scholars Gathering in a Bamboo Garden, 12th century. Primary source.

Question 9 · Look Closely. (2 pts) Describe what is happening in Source C in one sentence. Then list two details (setting, objects, clothing, people serving) that suggest wealth or leisure.

Question 10 · Purpose and Audience. (2 pts) Is Source C an idealized picture or a realistic record of an actual gathering? Support your answer with one detail. Then explain how this picture of golden age China differs from Source B.

Early Finisher · Source DYan Zhitui, Family Instructions

Optional. Every source in this assignment was made by a man. Yan Zhitui (531–591), a scholar-official, wrote these instructions for his own family just before the Tang dynasty began.

In the state, women should not be allowed to participate in politics; in the family, they should not be permitted to meddle in others’ affairs. If they are wise, talented and versed in the ancient and modern writings, they ought to help their husbands by supplementing the latter’s deficiency. No hen should herald the dawn lest misfortune follow. . . .
The burden of daughters on the family is heavy indeed. Yet since heaven gives life to the teeming people and ancestors transmit physical traits, what can be done about it? Many people today dislike their daughters and mistreat their own flesh and blood. Is it right for them to do so . . . ?

Excerpted from Yen Chih-T’ui, Family Instructions for the Yen Clan, trans. Teng Ssu-Yü (Leiden: Brill, 1968).

D1 · Point of View. (optional) What roles does Yan Zhitui believe women should and should not have? What does he suggest about how families treated daughters?

D2 · Explain. (optional) All the sources in this assignment were created by men. Use Source D and one earlier source to explain what we can and cannot learn about women’s experiences in golden age China.
